Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 11 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 625 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

Draft:

Summer projects are meant to keep students learning while school is out, but a project only works if the student actually cares about it. For that reason, summer projects should be student-designed, with teachers providing guidance, standards, and a check on quality. A student who chooses the question, the method, and the final product is far more likely to spend the summer thinking hard about something real than one who is handed a worksheet with a new cover page.

The strongest argument for student design is ownership. When a student picks a topic, the work stops being homework and becomes a question the student wants answered. Consider a sixteen-year-old who loves baking and decides to investigate why sourdough bread rises differently in summer humidity than in winter. She must form a hypothesis, measure flour hydration and room temperature, keep a log, and explain her results. She learns chemistry, data collection, and writing, and she does so because the project belongs to her. A teacher-designed assignment on the same skills, such as summarizing three chapters of a textbook, rarely produces the same engagement.

Student-designed projects also build skills that teacher-designed ones cannot easily reach. Choosing a project requires narrowing a broad interest into a question that can be finished in ten weeks, which is a difficult and useful skill. Students must plan their own timelines, decide when they are stuck, and ask for help. These are the habits that matter in college and in work, where nobody hands out a neatly packaged assignment with a rubric attached. A summer spent designing a project is practice for that independence.

Critics argue that students will choose easy projects or waste the summer on things they already know. This concern is legitimate, but it is solved by structure rather than by taking away choice. A teacher can require a proposal, a mid-summer check-in, and a final presentation, and can reject projects that do not meet a clear standard of difficulty or evidence. A student who wants to build a video game can still be asked to document the programming concepts they learned, measure how long each feature took, and explain what they would change. The teacher's role shifts from designing the content to guiding the thinking, which is a better use of a teacher's expertise.

Equity is another consideration. Some students arrive at summer with access to libraries, mentors, and equipment, while others do not. Teacher-designed projects can seem fairer because everyone receives the same task, but in practice identical tasks produce unequal results depending on home resources. A student-designed project can be scaled to the resources a student actually has. A student without a laboratory can study the local water quality of a nearby creek with a cheap testing kit, or interview grandparents about changes in their neighborhood. Choice allows a project to fit the life the student is living.

Finally, student-designed work is more honest about what learning looks like. Students who design their own projects often discover that their first question was wrong, that their data were incomplete, or that their conclusion needed revision. Those moments of failure and revision are where durable learning happens. A teacher-designed project tends to have a predictable answer, which may leave students performing the steps without understanding why they matter.

Teachers still have an important role. Their knowledge keeps projects rigorous, their feedback helps students refine their questions, and their standards keep the work meaningful. But the central decision, what to study and why, should belong to the student. Summer is the one stretch of the year when a student is free from the usual schedule of assignments. Using that time to pursue a question the student genuinely wants to answer is the most reliable way to keep learning alive.
